questions.q: What does a partial derivative ∂f/∂x1 compute?
options: The rate of change of f with respect to x1, holding all other variables fixed
The total change in f summed over all variables
The average value of f over its domain
The second derivative of f with respect to x1
questions.explain: A partial derivative differentiates with respect to one variable while treating every other variable as a constant.

questions.q: What key geometric property does the gradient vector ∇f(x) have?
options: It always has length 1
It points in the direction of steepest increase of f at that point
It is always perpendicular to the x-axis
It is only defined for linear functions
questions.explain: The gradient points toward the direction in which f increases fastest; its negative points toward the steepest decrease, which drives gradient descent.

questions.q: In option pricing, vega is best described as which object?
options: The second derivative of value with respect to the stock price
The partial derivative of option value with respect to volatility
The integral of the payoff over time
The Jacobian of the entire options book
questions.explain: Vega measures sensitivity of option value to volatility while other inputs (like price) are held fixed — exactly a partial derivative.

questions.q: What does the Hessian matrix of a scalar function represent?
options: The vector of first partial derivatives
The matrix of all second partial derivatives, describing curvature
The determinant of the gradient
A list of the function's roots
questions.explain: The Hessian collects all second partial derivatives, H_ij = ∂²f/∂xi∂xj, and describes how the function curves; it is symmetric when second partials are continuous.

questions.q: In the gradient descent update w = w - lr * grad_f(w), why do we subtract the gradient rather than add it?
options: Subtraction is computationally cheaper than addition
Because the gradient points toward steepest increase, so moving opposite it decreases the function
It has no effect on convergence either way
Because gradients are always negative numbers
questions.explain: Since ∇f points toward steepest increase, stepping in the direction -∇f moves toward steepest decrease, which is exactly how gradient descent minimizes a function.
